executive_assessment.text: Salani and Vaitele show different land-tenure and mobility contexts; Matafa'a and Salei'a provide historical, programme-reported capacity examples.
Lalomanu livelihood trade-offs and caveated protection concerns require careful trigger and sample qualification; PREPARE adds prospective Sālelologa land/inclusion safeguards.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2023-09-18 reports: Rural coastal Salani had 93% of 88 households on customary land; inland suburban Vaitele had 80% of about 1,300 households on freehold land.
Source dated 2023-09-18 reports: At Salani, 10/20 participants partly or fully linked inland moves to climate factors (four entirely); storm surge and cyclone rainfall were recurring triggers.

Source dated 2023-09-18 reports: At Vaitele, 6/20 households linked movement partly or fully to climate factors; seven participants cited social reasons and seven freehold access, with overlap in environmental changes.
Source dated 2023-09-18 reports: Seventeen of 20 Salani households near water moved inland; short moves were easier where customary access avoided land-purchase costs.

Source dated 2019-10-28 reports: UNDP described Salei'a as exposed to sea-level rise, flooding, erosion, stronger tropical storms, rainfall and heat; by 2019 a revetment and raised bridge provided daily access and a disaster escape route.

Source dated 2017 reports: At Matafa'a, runoff, land management, variable rain, floods and drought were linked to poor water quality and livelihood and health effects; elderly people, women and children bore water-collection burdens.

Source dated 2017 reports: The report says a mountain gravity-fed system and native reforestation were installed; Matafa'a had water during the three-month September 2011 El Niño drought, with clean water in all homes.
Source dated 2017 reports: Matafa'a's community-managed scheme set a household maintenance fee; the Independent Water Scheme Association supported filter maintenance and water quality.
Source dated 2024-06-30 reports: Women at a Lalomanu workshop said inland relocation reduced sea access and coastal-road customers for craft and seafood businesses.
Source dated 2025-06 reports: In June 2025, PREPARE planned six years of hazard monitoring, early warning, response and urban resilience work, with township planning focused on Sālelologa.

Source dated 2025-06 reports: The ESMF identifies Sālelologa land disputes as a potential planning conflict risk; proposed controls map disputes, exclude disputed areas and use consultation and grievance handling.
Source dated 2025-06 reports: The ESMF flags possible exclusion of women, youth, people with disabilities and other marginalized groups from Sālelologa planning.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification or human approval. 18 of 19 evidence records and 0 of 0 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.
No countrywide causal estimate of climate impacts on conflict or violence is established by these sources.
Full subnational coverage and independently evaluated long-term response effectiveness remain gaps.
Tsunami exposure mentioned in multi-hazard sources is not classified as a climate hazard.
Draft collection pending human source review and approval. IDA eligibility is not an FCV classification.
National and selected local examples do not establish district-level coverage or causal attribution.
The bank contains no completed mediated climate-FCV pathway; this is an evidence gap, not evidence of absence.
No directly read Samoa source established that climate change caused violent conflict; the domestic-violence signal in the Pacific synthesis is explicitly caveated and non-causal.

The 2025 PREPARE land-dispute and inclusion statements are preliminary planning risks, not realized project impacts; project status should be refreshed before treating planned safeguards as implemented.
UNDP and GEF SGP community results are programme-reported rather than independently evaluated; Matafa'a water findings refer to the 2011 drought and project-era conditions.
The 2017 Samoa Ombudsman climate-rights report was excluded from findings because its reuse notice requires permission for external/public use.
Lalomanu relocation accounts do not establish the hazard trigger; tsunami-related movement must not be classified as climate-caused.
Qualitative domestic-violence signals cannot support a countrywide trend or climate-to-violence causal pathway.
Draft extension: human source review and approval remain pending. Lending eligibility is not an FCV classification.
